title: Finite-stage inclusion preserves the canonical tensor/pullback square
statement: Fix a finite-field datum D, coefficient datum C, common stages H, finite coefficient field E, and compactified square Q [def-sf-operation-stages]. Transport the supplied rational and common tensor/pullback comparisons into the named operation coordinates using their functor equalities. Curry the canonical finite-stage inclusion tensorator [def-sf-common-projection-tensor-comparison]. These four tensor comparisons are ComparisonCompatible with the inverse of the prescribed pullback comparison (H.commonStageComparison E).directAdjunction Q.p. This is the tensor/pullback square on every pair of rational inputs on Q.Y, with the canonical comparisons of [def-pur-completed-pullback-tensor-comparison]; it involves no support functor, direct image, projection mate, or counit.

proof.text: Normalize the rational and common pullback and tensor functors by the recorded equalities. The supplied tensor/pullback components are the canonical ones by the two tensorPullbackNormalization fields. The coefficient pullback comparison is the identity on the prescribed object models by commonStageModelNormalization. The transport and currying definitions only re-express these same arrows.

For two rational inputs included from E, evaluate canonicalCommonStagePullbackTensor at the common finite field E. Expand pullbackTensorAtCommonStage: the pullback transition at the tensor, pullback of the tensor transition, the rational tensor/pullback comparison, tensor of inverse pullback transitions, and inverse final tensor transition. Express the two canonical inclusion tensorators by commonInclusionTensorModel and the scalar unit of the repeated transition E to E. Naturality of the transition maps and canonicalRationalPullbackTensor_scalar identify both composites after cancelling the intermediate transition maps. Apply ofHom at E to obtain the common-stage equality. Transport back along the normalization equalities to obtain ComparisonCompatible. The same formulas cover zero objects, empty schemes and identities.
